title: Phase transitions as cellular decision points across stress granules, P-bodies, and nucleoli
abstract:
This working group asks how phase transitions as cellular decision points across stress granules, p-bodies, and nucleoli can be understood as an emergent property that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. The scientific question is not simply whether particular molecules, organelles, or pathways are associated with a phenotype, but whether publicly available datasets can reveal rules by which many molecular parts collectively produce a new, system-level behavior at the scale between biomolecules and organelles. The project is designed for the NCEMS model because the relevant evidence is scattered across incompatible imaging repositories, omics studies, perturbation resources, structural annotations, and specialized literatures; no single laboratory is likely to have the biological breadth, data-engineering capacity, and methodological expertise to integrate them.

The group would synthesize existing public data centered on imaging + proteomics, prioritizing datasets with reusable metadata, perturbation or state annotations, and links to downstream cellular phenotypes. Depending on availability, sources could include public cell atlases, the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas, EMBL-EBI and NCBI functional genomics repositories, BioImage Archive or Image Data Resource collections, PRIDE/MassIVE proteomics datasets, public CRISPR or RNAi screens, AlphaFold/PDB-derived structural features, and curated pathway or protein-interaction resources. The core analytic strategy would be causal discovery: harmonizing measurements into a common representation; explicitly modeling uncertainty, batch effects, and missingness; and testing whether mesoscale variables explain cellular outcomes above and beyond molecular abundance alone. The biological scope would focus on cross-kingdom/cross-species while deliberately including comparison cases that prevent the group from mistaking a narrow model-system pattern for a general law.

The novel element is the unit of explanation. Instead of treating mesoscale organization as an image label, downstream readout, or anecdotal mechanism, the working group would make it the primary object of synthesis: a measurable layer where composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion combine. The expected product is a predictive atlas that is open, versioned, and reusable, with transparent workflows, community-agreed metadata standards, and tutorials for trainees. The project would bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics researchers, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, data curators, and trainees across institution types. Training would occur through hackathon-style data sprints, reproducible workflow clinics, and rotating trainee leadership of cross-dataset validation tasks. The anticipated contribution is both scientific and infrastructural: a defensible answer to a specific emergence question, plus a generalizable synthesis strategy that helps the molecular and cellular biosciences reuse public data to discover phenomena that only become visible when datasets, disciplines, and scales are brought together.
